#104849. The $500 billion beauty industry's 'green' ambitions are a patchwork at best. And they're falling short

📅 03 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1682 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNN ↗ Open Full Page

The $500 billion beauty industry's 'green' ambitions are a patchwork at best. And they're falling short

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1682 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The escalating climate crisis is shifting many people’s purchasing patterns and this extends to the $500 billion dollar global beauty industry which is grappling with a range of sustainability challenges across product manufacturing, packaging and disposal.
  • 'Delay means death': We're running out of ways to adapt to the climate crisis, newly introduced report indicates.
  • Strategy and consulting firm Simon Kucher’s Global Sustainability Study 2021 found 60% of consumers around the world rated sustainability as an notable purchase criterion, and 35% were willing to pay more for sustainable products or services.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The escalating climate crisis is shifting many people’s purchasing patterns and this extends to the $500 billion dollar global beauty industry which is grappling with a range of sustainability challenges across product manufacturing, packaging and disposal.

'Delay means death': We're running out of ways to adapt to the climate crisis, newly introduced report indicates. Here are the key takeaways.

Strategy and consulting firm Simon Kucher’s Global Sustainability Study 2021 found 60% of consumers around the world rated sustainability as an notable purchase criterion, and 35% were willing to pay more for sustainable products or services.

This shift in consumer preferences has propelled many beauty brands to set environmental goals: to move away from single-use and virgin plastics, provide recyclable, reusable and refillable packaging and offer more transparency around products’ ingredients so customers can ascertain how “green” their purchase is.

However, consumers still struggle to understand the sustainability credentials of many products, according to the British Beauty Council. This is because the industry’s clean-up efforts have been inconsistent, and fall short of making a recognizable impact in the absence of collective goal-setting, global strategy and standardized regulations.

It has been revealed that there is no international standard for the beauty industry on how much product ingredient information to share with customers — or how to do so. Brands can set their own rules and goals, giving rise to confusion and “greenwashing,” where sustainability claims are often touted but not substantiated.

Companies often use marketing language like “clean beauty” to make it seem like their products are natural, for example, when they may not actually be organic, sustainable or ethically made.

After rebranding in the West, many beauty companies are still offering to 'whiten' skin elsewhere.

Recent findings suggest that “The term ‘clean beauty’ has become quite dangerous. It’s used to sell more products,” according to British Beauty Council CEO Millie Kendall, who added that such buzzwords are losing traction in the UK as British customers wise up to their shortcomings. “Customers need better marketing information and certification information.”.

In a 2021 report calling on the industry to have “the courage to change” their business practices, the British Beauty Council wrote that, all too often, even natural ingredients involved in manufacturing products give way to “over-consumption, non-regenerative farming practices, pollution, waste and neglect.”.

“The only way out of this is transparency,” Kendall told CNN.

Industry observers note that jen Lee, chief impact officer at US-based brand Beautycounter, said she continues to see confusion over ingredients among consumers. (In 2013, the company debuted and published “The Never List,” which currently cites more than 2,800 chemicals — including heavy metals, parabens and formaldehyde — it claims to never use in its products.).

Recent findings suggest that “Natural vs. synthetic ingredients has been a conversation. People think natural is safer, but it’s not always the case,” Lee explained. “Natural ingredients formulated in the industry can have toxic load. Heavy metals can occur in natural components of the earth.”.

Mother loses peripheral vision from apparent exposure to mercury in beauty creams. Toxic levels in her home put family at risk, say experts.

“We used to be more natural and organic,” added Sasha Plavsic, founder of makeup brand ILIA Beauty. “What was challenging is (that) raw materials were difficult to source or would come in inconsistently or products wouldn’t perform.”.

In a recent development, most makeup is created and molded at high temperatures, Plavsic explained. Purely organic materials often fall apart in this heat, leading to inconsistent results and subpar product performance. “Not every synthetic is bad,” Plavsic said. “Sometimes, it helps create the best in class formula.”.

The industry’s plastic packaging is a particular sustainability challenge — 95% is thrown away and the vast majority is not recycled, according to the British Beauty Council.

It has been revealed that the cosmetics business is the fourth biggest plastic packaging user globally — after food and beverage, industrial packaging and pharmaceuticals — and plastic is about 67% of the industry’s packaging volume, according to Vantage Market Research. Beauty giant L’Oreal used 144,430 metric tons of plastic in its packaging material in 2021, for example, according to the Ellen Macarthur Foundation (EMF). Estee Lauder Companies reported its brands produced 71,600 metric tons of plastic in product packaging that same year.

In a recent development, and only 9% of the global plastic waste is recycled, according to a report from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. The United States only recycles 4% of its plastic waste.

According to recent reports, single-use plastic is wreaking havoc on the planet. Here's what you can do to minimize your impact.

Many brands are trying to phase out harmful plastics from their operations and adopt post-consumer recycled (PCR) plastic. (L’Oreal has set a target of 50% PCR plastic usage by 2025, while Estee Lauder is targeting 25% “or more” PCR plastic — but both are far from achieving their targets.).

“Between 60-70 major global brands have made unprecedented progress” in PCR plastic usage across industries, EMF’s Plastic Initiative Lead Sander DeFruyt told CNN. But DeFruyt stressed that PCR plastic must be adopted in conjunction with brands removing single and virgin plastics from their usage cycles to truly make a difference.

However, PCR plastic is not easy to find — low recycling rates around the world mean there is limited supply. Meanwhile, demand for it is growing demand across industries, DeFruyt said. This competition hikes up its price, which is already higher than virgin plastic.

Hair care brand FEKKAI claims that it used up to 95% PCR content in its packaging, but pricing and supply complications posed a challenge, forcing it to currently aim for containers and packaging that feature at least 50% PCR in its packaging.

Sources indicate that “PCR plastic is more expensive than stock plastic. The cost is hard and then sourcing it is too,” founder Frédéric Fekkai told CNN. “PCR is close to our heart, but there is a massive demand, so finding recycled plastic is difficult.”.

Industry observers note that beauty retailers plays a pivotal — and under-utilized — role, with control over stocking decisions and supply chains. But many vary when it comes to the standards they set for brands they sell.

“Smaller businesses do more, full stop,” noted Jessi Baker, founder of the technology platform Provenance, which helps brands display their sustainability credentials for customers. “They move more nimbly. Some of them are born-good brands — climate friendliness was part of their setup. They don’t need to restructure their entire supply chain. Their culture already has it compared to the larger brands who need to work hard to change.”.

A history of beauty trends -- and the standards that shaped them.

It has been revealed that sephora released its “Clean + Planet Positive” initiative in 2021, which labeled products that met its set criteria. (This is separate from the French retailer’s “Clean at Sephora” program, which is right now facing a consumer lawsuit alleging it carries a significant percentage of products understood by customers to be harmful.) Target launched a similar program in 2022, featuring a “Target Zero” icon for both online and in-store offerings that either have reusable, recyclable, compostable or reduced plastic packaging, or feature waterless or concentrated products.

Still, many steps taken by brands and retailers do not even begin to touch on the waste and pollution generated throughout supply chains, manufacturing and shipping, all huge problems for the industry to grapple with.

The gaps in standardization in the beauty ecosystem can, to some extent, be filled by certifications such as the US-born B Corporation, or B Corp. This accreditation, one of the most well-known in the beauty space, is issued by the non-profit B Lab, which scores a company on a variety of criteria around ethics and sustainability. However beneficial it may be among eco-conscious consumers, though, it is right now completely voluntary for brands to apply for.

Governments and multinationals enforcing regulations and setting a base line for brands to operate from when making sustainability claims would go a long way to making change, many experts and business leaders believe.

Susanne Kaufmann, founder of her namesake beauty brand, claims her efforts in Austria would reap better results if more countries around the world had stricter, more uniform garbage disposal laws.

A trash heap 62 meters high highlights the scale of India's climate challenge.

Sources indicate that “I package our product in a recyclable material,” Kaufmann said. (Her products’ packaging, which is refillable and reusable, is made from 75% recycled plastic — and is 100% recyclable.) If I send this to the US, the garbage is not separated… and it’s not recyclable,” she explained, referring to inconsistencies in recycling laws across the United States.

Sources indicate that and when it comes to ingredients, the European Chemicals Agency lists 2,495 substances banned from use in cosmetic products marketed for sale or use in the bloc. But the US Food and Drug administration only lists 11, making it more challenging for American consumers to find safer, greener options. The Environmental Working Group, a non-profit watchdog, studied lab tests of 51 sunscreen products in 2021 and found that only 35% of products met the EU standard, compared with 94% that passed the US standard.

However, while government can set minimum requirements, Mia Davis, vice president of sustainability and impact at beauty retailer Credo Beauty, notes the needle will move in the private sector.

Sustainable ships: The world's most eco-conscious cruises.

“Regulation can raise the floor a bit. A person who doesn’t know about any (sustainability concerns) should still be able to walk into a bodega and get clean products… But that’s never going to be what the market can do,” she said. “Market leadership is key.”.

In a recent development, in the absence of bold regulations or global standards on sustainability practices, this “leadership” — undertaken both by brands and customers in the beauty marketplace — is likely to be the most immediately impactful vector for addressing the industry’s climate shortcomings. It will take continued collective advocacy and initiative to see meaningful climate-conscious change.

Industry News: NASA Eyes Crop Candidates for Future Menus

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (653 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nasa

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that as NASA prepares for future missions to the Moon and Mars, researchers are studying crops that could provide astronauts with fresh food, nutrition, and variety far from Earth.
  • Recent findings suggest that recent testing points to strawberries, cucumbers, and lemon basil as potential options for future explorers.
  • Recent findings suggest that while space crop research advances on Earth, capabilities are also expanding in space.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that as NASA prepares for future missions to the Moon and Mars, researchers are studying crops that could provide astronauts with fresh food, nutrition, and variety far from Earth. Such crop variety can help with menus in deep space, something top of mind this week as the nation celebrates Thanksgiving.

Recent findings suggest that recent testing points to strawberries, cucumbers, and lemon basil as potential options for future explorers. Space crops can absorb carbon dioxide, produce oxygen, and recycle water. These capabilities will become increasingly important as crewed missions extend farther from our home planet.

Recent findings suggest that while space crop research advances on Earth, capabilities are also expanding in space. A new investigation from NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division is set to launch to the International Space Station, where the first-of-its-kind prototype growth chamber will provide critical insights for developing crop production systems that could grow crops like these for future Moon Base habitats and Mars missions.

Strawberries are among the few sweet fruits under consideration for spaceflight and are nutritious, aromatic, and self-pollinating.

Researchers at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida are growing strawberries in flight-like growth chambers to evaluate the potential space crop, and NASA partners at The Australian Research Council Centre for Excellence in Plants for Space also are helping expand knowledge of space strawberries.

Researchers at NASA Kennedy, the University of Melbourne, and the University of Western Australia recently tested a wild strawberry against NASA’s leading strawberry candidate, ‘Delizz,’ to see which thrived better under simulated space conditions.

Recent findings suggest that delizz and the wild strawberry produced very different fruits, according to a study published in September in the journal Life Sciences in Space Research. Delizz grew large, red fruit, while the wild strawberry produced small, yellow fruit due to a recessive genetic mutation.

In a recent development, but looks are not everything. When grown from a seed, the wild strawberry produced twice as many buds, flowers, and fruit as Delizz. Ultimately, however, NASA’s pick kept its top spot, as the wild strawberry grew too many runners that would take up valuable room aboard a spacecraft.

Industry observers note that many crops have been grown in space, but none so far have come from the gourd family. Cucumbers could be the first.

Before crops like cucumbers can be grown and eaten in space, they must undergo extensive testing. NASA-funded researchers recently evaluated cucumbers for their growth, yield, and nutrition under spaceflight conditions.

The researchers found that while the plants showed some signs of enlarged leaves, they produced a steady stream of edible fruit, according to a study published in August in the journal HortScience.

Offering a variety of crops, such as cucumbers, not only benefits astronauts’ diets and mental well-being, but it also increases plant biodiversity, which can improve the likelihood of crop success on long-duration missions.

Herbs can spice up life in space, turning a bland meal into a bold one.

Lemon basil, an edible herb with a citrus scent and taste, is making strides in testing at NASA Kennedy.

Researchers report that lemon basil passed its preliminary round of space crop testing and successfully underwent seed sanitization, which is required before spaceflight to remove microorganisms from the seeds. Lemon basil’s next steps include assessing its growth in plant pillows, which can house plants aboard the space station.

Menu fatigue can quickly become a problem for astronauts, but fresh herbs like lemon basil help transform packaged meals into something new and satisfying, supporting human health and performance in space.

Sources indicate that NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division pioneers scientific discovery and enables exploration by using space environments to conduct investigations not possible on Earth. Studying biological and physical phenomena under extreme conditions allows researchers to advance the fundamental scientific knowledge required to go farther and stay longer in space, while also benefitting life on Earth.

Industry News: Physicists trap antimatter in a breakthrough that could explain why the universe exists

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1252 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, physicists at Northwestern University have achieved an unprecedented level of quantum control over a single positron, the antimatter counterpart of an electron.
  • The researchers captured a rapidly moving positron produced through radioactive decay, slowed it down, and cooled it to a temperature just above absolute zero.
  • Using this approach, the team created what they call a "one-positron quantum cyclotron." Within this system, the positron behaves somewhat like an artificial atom, allowing researchers to observe and precisely manipulate its individual quantum energy levels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, physicists at Northwestern University have achieved an unprecedented level of quantum control over a single positron, the antimatter counterpart of an electron. The breakthrough could eventually help scientists answer one of the most fundamental questions in physics: Why does the universe exist as we know it?

The researchers captured a rapidly moving positron produced through radioactive decay, slowed it down, and cooled it to a temperature just above absolute zero. They then confined the particle within a near-perfect vacuum, isolating it from ordinary matter, which would cause it to annihilate.

Using this approach, the team created what they call a "one-positron quantum cyclotron." Within this system, the positron behaves somewhat like an artificial atom, allowing researchers to observe and precisely manipulate its individual quantum energy levels.

Recent findings suggest that the achievement lays the groundwork for what could become the most rigorous test yet of the fundamental symmetry between electrons and positrons. The Standard Model of particle physics predicts that the two particles should behave as nearly perfect mirror images of each other.

By measuring the positron's magnetic properties with unprecedented accuracy and comparing them with those of an electron, scientists could uncover previously undetected differences. Any unexpected discrepancy would point to a weakness in the Standard Model and potentially offer clues to why the universe contains so much more matter than antimatter.

The research was published in Physical Review Letters.

It has been revealed that "Antimatter gets its popular charm from science fiction," mentioned Northwestern's Gerald Gabrielse, who led the study. "If you take an electron and an anti-electron (or positron) and collide them together, they both disappear. We describe that as annihilation, a concept that fuels science fiction writers' imaginations. The major mystery of the universe is the Big Bang should have created equal amounts of matter and antimatter. But, if that were true, it would annihilate, and we'd be left with nothing. There's clearly something wrong with that theory, and that's what we're trying to figure out.".

Gabrielse is the Board of Trustees Professor of Physics at Northwestern's Weinberg College of Arts and Sciences and director of the university's Center for Fundamental Physics. Thomas Myers, a Ph.D. student working in Gabrielse's laboratory, is the study's first author.

Searching for Cracks in the Standard Model.

The Standard Model is one of the most successful theories in modern science. It describes the universe's fundamental particles and three of its four fundamental forces (electromagnetic, strong nuclear and weak nuclear forces). Countless experiments have verified its predictions with remarkable accuracy.

Sources indicate that despite those successes, the theory remains incomplete. One of its most significant shortcomings is its inability to explain the overwhelming abundance of matter compared with antimatter in the observable universe.

"We know the Standard Model has to be wrong somewhere -- or at least incomplete," Gabrielse said. "For example, it cannot predict why the universe exists, so that's a pretty massive loophole. We're very precisely examining the most fundamental and simple systems to find where the theory breaks down. We hope to find an unambiguous answer.".

Gabrielse has devoted decades of his scientific career to investigating this mystery. His research group previously developed methods for isolating individual electrons and determining their magnetic properties with exceptional precision.

In a recent development, he also helped establish the field of low-energy antimatter research by pioneering techniques for slowing, capturing, and cooling antiprotons. The latest achievement combines these two areas of expertise, extending the sophisticated quantum control previously demonstrated with electrons to an individual antimatter particle.

Trapping Antimatter Without Touching It.

According to recent reports, almost everything on Earth is composed of three familiar particles: electrons, protons, and neutrons. A universe made of antimatter could contain their respective counterparts: positrons, antiprotons, and antineutrons. According to Gabrielse, if everything on Earth were constructed from antimatter instead of ordinary matter, distinguishing between the two would be remarkably difficult.

It has been revealed that the dramatic differences emerge when matter and antimatter come into contact. An electron and a positron, for example, can annihilate when they encounter one another. This makes storing antimatter particularly challenging, as contact with the material walls of an ordinary container would almost certainly destroy the trapped particle.

According to recent reports, "If we want to study antimatter, we must handle it carefully," Gabrielse said. "To be clear, it's not dangerous. We don't have enough antimatter to make an explosion.".

To overcome this problem, the Northwestern researchers employed an advanced particle trap that uses carefully configured electric and magnetic fields. These fields keep the positron suspended in an empty region of space, preventing it from coming into contact with the surrounding material.

By effectively creating a container that does not require the particle to touch any physical walls, the team has managed to keep a single positron confined in Gabrielse's laboratory for months.

Cooling Antimatter to Near Absolute Zero.

In a recent development, capturing a positron presents another considerable technical hurdle. Certain atomic nuclei release positrons as they undergo radioactive decay. For their experiment, the researchers used sodium-22, a rare radioactive isotope of sodium. Positrons emitted during this process initially carry tremendous amounts of energy.

The physicists substantially reduced the particle's speed before directing it into the trap's near-perfect vacuum. Inside, the temperature is maintained at approximately 300 millikelvins, equivalent to just 0.3 degrees above absolute zero.

Under these extremely cold conditions, the positron can settle into its lowest possible quantum energy state.

"We cool it down so much that it's in its quantum ground state," Gabrielse stated. "We actually coaxed this very fast positron to sit there and behave for months at a time.".

Putting Matter and Antimatter to the Ultimate Test.

Beyond capturing and cooling the positron, the researchers demonstrated that they could deliberately change its individual quantum energy states and detect those changes.

Recent findings suggest that using microwaves tuned to specific frequencies, the physicists transferred carefully controlled amounts of energy to the particle and observed the resulting transitions between quantum states. This ability is crucial to their larger objective of determining the positron's magnetic properties with exceptional accuracy and comparing them directly with those of an electron.

Recent findings suggest that in earlier research, Gabrielse and his colleagues used a one-electron quantum cyclotron to determine the electron's magnetic moment, a measure of its magnetic properties, with a precision of approximately one part in 10 trillion. That achievement ranks among the most precise measurements ever performed on an elementary particle.

It has been revealed that the team now intends to conduct an equivalent measurement using the trapped positron. Comparing the two results could provide an extraordinarily sensitive test of current particle physics theories and potentially uncover evidence of previously unknown physics.

It has been revealed that "Current theories suggest that there will be no difference in the two measurements," Gabrielse said. "If it turns out they are not equal, that would be the biggest discovery in physics in the last century.".

The study, "One-positron quantum cyclotron," received support from the National Science Foundation (grant number 2110565).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Significant pizza chains are struggling as weaker consumer spending, a wider variety of dining options and the rise of GLP-1 medications weigh on their sales.

It has been revealed that the pandemic was a boom time for Domino's Pizza, Papa Johns, Little Caesars and Pizza Hut. But since dining rooms reopened, the biggest U.S. pizza chains have faced an uphill battle to retain their customers.

These days, consumers are watching their discretionary spending but have more delivery and takeout options when they do decide to order, thanks to the accessibility of third-party platforms. Plus, food quality and the customer experience have become more crucial to diners who are looking for value when they order from restaurants.

In a recent development, as a result of pizza fatigue and challenges facing the broader restaurant industry, the number of U.S. pizza restaurants has tumbled. Since pizza locations hit a peak of 83,035 nationwide in August 2019, more than 9,600 pizzerias had closed their doors as of July 2026, according to data from Datassential.

In a recent development, in 2025, sales at U.S. pizza restaurants fell 0.3%, according to Technomic data. Sales at independent pizzerias slipped 0.4%. Chains, which account for about two-thirds of the domestic pizza category sales, saw revenue shrink 0.3%.

Papa Johns reported that North American same-store sales declined 2.5% in 2025. Pizza Hut's U.S. same-store sales fell 5%. Among the three pizza chains that were publicly traded last year, only Domino's posted annual same-store sales growth at its U.S. restaurants, with an increase of 3%.

Sources indicate that it isn't just diners who have lost their appetite for pizza. Since March 2020, Papa Johns stock has lost about two-thirds of its value. Even shares of Domino's, which dominates the category, have seen gains of only about 2% in that time. For comparison, the S&P 500 has climbed about 150% over the same period.

And Yum Brands sold Pizza Hut this year, offloading the laggard of its portfolio to LongRange Capital and Yum China after about two decades of stagnating sales.

In a recent development, "Pizza Hut has been a detractor for YUM ... Going forward, YUM won't be tripped up by pizza category dynamics (discounting, etc.), translating to stronger growth and higher concentration in higher growth industry segments and markets," Wells Fargo analyst Zachary Fadem wrote in a research note in September.

Pizza chains now have significantly more competition for diners' dollars than they did in 2020. Third-party delivery platforms, which grew in popularity during the pandemic, offer a wide variety of cuisines beyond the traditional pizza and Chinese. As a result, Domino's and Papa John's have to compete with other fast-food chains, like McDonald's and Chick-fil-A, for DoorDash and Uber Eats orders.

As pizza has grown more expensive, a pie seems less appealing to budget-conscious diners. The average large cheese pizza is now almost $17, according to the 2026 Pizza Power Report from PMQ Pizza, a trade publication.

Plus, frozen pizza is another convenient option, with a lower price tag. Retail sales of single- and multi-serve frozen pizza rose 2.9% in the 52 weeks ended Nov. 7 compared with the same period in 2022, according to NielsenIQ data.

"When the American consumer is focused on the least expensive eating occasion, the items that are in my pantry, my refrigerator and my freezer win every single time," noted David Portalatin, a food and food service industry advisor for Circana.

Convenience stores like Casey's General Stores have also won over customers with pizza at a low price point.

"We believe that [Casey's] has an advantage over [quick-service restaurants] and dollar stores, which have fewer options to navigate the persistent inflationary environment, while [Casey's] can offset food pressures with margins," Bank of America Securities analyst Sara Senatore wrote in a research note published in June.

She added that geographic overlap of locations suggests that Casey's is stealing share from Pizza Hut.

The biggest pizza chains have also been slow to adapt to shifting consumer attitudes toward nutrition. For example, of the four biggest chains, Papa Johns is the only one to even test a pizza crust with added protein as more diners prioritize it in their diets. And the test was only in one Atlanta restaurant — for a single day.

Recent findings suggest that pizza's nutritional content more broadly is another drag for the category. Its carbohydrate and fat content, from its dough and cheese, respectively, can make it less appealing for consumers on GLP-1 drugs, which have skyrocketed in use over the last several years.

Spending on pizza quick-service restaurants has fallen 22.2% per GLP-1 household after six to eight months using the medications, according to a 2026 survey published by PwC.

To be sure, pizza's recent struggles do not mean an existential crisis for the category. Total pizza servings are down only about 1% this year, Circana's Portalatin said.

And chains are trying to reverse that downturn in servings. In August, Domino's rolled out the Domino, a customizable Detroit-style personal pizza to attract solo diners. In November, Papa Johns unveiled a new turnaround initiative focusing on improving food consistency and restaurant operations. And Pizza Hut is running a holiday-themed meal deal.

Industry observers note that "Pizza's not going anywhere," Portalatin noted. "The American consumer loves pizza.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How NASA works with small businesses is evolving, and as a result, the agency is strengthening the domestic aerospace industrial base to support future exploration missions through its recently renamed Small Business Supplier Development Program. As part of the program, NASA announced its latest Mentor-Protégé Agreement, this one signed between The Boeing Tech giant and GRACE Aerospace.

According to recent reports, NASA is streamlining the application process for the Small Business Supplier Development Program, as well as reducing administrative requirements, accelerating review and approval timelines, and enhancing incentives for prime contractor participation. These improvements are aimed at making supplier development more accessible, efficient, and closely aligned with NASA’s mission needs.

It has been revealed that “We have intentionally redesigned the program as a mission-focused tool for strengthening industrial base readiness and mission success,” said Dwight Deneal, assistant administrator, Office of Small Business Programs, NASA Headquarters in Washington. “By simplifying participation and focusing developmental assistance on the capabilities NASA needs most, we are helping build a stronger, more resilient supplier base that can support the agency’s highest-priority missions.”.

Under the latest Mentor-Protégé Agreement, Boeing will provide structured assistance to help GRACE expand its capabilities as a supplier of mission-critical aerospace hardware. Boeing will fund the agreement, valued at nearly $500,000.

“Boeing is proud to continue its longstanding relationship with NASA in support of its mission and the opportunities this agreement creates for Boeing, GRACE, and the broader aerospace industrial base,” said Christian Diamond, Mentor-Protégé Program manager and small business liaison officer for Boeing. “Through this partnership, Boeing looks forward to sharing our expertise to support the continued growth and long-term success of a small business while strengthening our supplier base.”.

Building on two decades of experience supporting defense and aerospace customers, GRACE will use the partnership to prepare for increasingly complex aerospace and spaceflight programs.

Sources indicate that “GRACE Aerospace is thankful and honored to participate in the program,” remarked Pauline Sevigny, president and owner of GRACE Aerospace. “We look forward to growing and learning from industry experts and supporting the mission of resilience and space superiority.”.

NASA’s enhanced supplier program is part of the agency’s broader Office of Small Business Programs.

https://www.nasa.gov/osbp/supplier-development-program/.

A space telescope hunting for dark matter just discovered something unexpected

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1148 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The European Space Agency's (ESA) Euclid space telescope has made an unexpected discovery in our own solar system.
  • In a recent development, the achievement is particularly remarkable given that Euclid was built to capture detailed images of distant galaxies rather than track rapidly moving objects such as comets.
  • Mikko Pöntinen, a PhD student at the University of Helsinki, made the discovery with the Solar System Objects Science Working Group of the Euclid Consortium.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The European Space Agency's (ESA) Euclid space telescope has made an unexpected discovery in our own solar system. Images captured between September 16 and 24, 2026, revealed a previously unknown comet, the first discovered by the mission.

In a recent development, the achievement is particularly remarkable given that Euclid was built to capture detailed images of distant galaxies rather than track rapidly moving objects such as comets. The speed with which researchers identified and confirmed the discovery demonstrates that Euclid can detect latest comets while they are still relatively far from the Sun. This capability could eventually help identify a target for ESA's upcoming Comet Interceptor mission.

A Mysterious Streak Reveals a Fresh Comet.

Mikko Pöntinen, a PhD student at the University of Helsinki, made the discovery with the Solar System Objects Science Working Group of the Euclid Consortium. Pöntinen developed specialized software to detect and track small solar system objects appearing in the telescope's images.

Industry observers note that "I was excited to see my software flag a 'streak' smeared across several images -- the result of a fast-moving object. By predicting its position I could identify it in other images, in total finding it in five image sets. Further inspection revealed that it had a fuzzy cloud around it, indicative of an active object like a comet that is shedding dust and gas.".

The object appeared in a region of the sky known as the 'Euclid Deep Field North'. Over several days, the telescope captured it in five separate fields of view, taking between two and four exposures of each field for a total of 16 exposures.

It has been revealed that after searching catalogs of known asteroids and comets without finding a match, Pöntinen submitted the observations to the International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center (MPC) as a potential fresh comet. The report enabled astronomers using telescopes on Earth to carry out additional observations. On October 8, the MPC officially confirmed the discovery. The comet has been designated C/2026 S1 (Euclid).

A Comet on an Extraordinary Orbit.

The newly discovered comet is approximately 1.3 billion kilometers (about 800 million miles) from Earth. That distance is comparable to the distance from the Sun to a point somewhere between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn.

However, the comet is traveling well outside the relatively flat plane in which the planets orbit the Sun. It is currently positioned almost directly above the Sun, following a sweeping path over the solar system that will take thousands of years to complete.

According to recent reports, the International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center (MPC) serves as the central international hub for observations of asteroids and comets. It gathers data from observers around the world to verify discoveries, determine orbital paths, and assign official designations. As additional observations become available, astronomers will be able to calculate the orbital period of C/2026 S1 (Euclid) more precisely.

Why Euclid Rarely Discovers New Comets.

Although Euclid has spotted comets before, all of them had already been discovered. Several aspects of the telescope's design and observing strategy make finding previously unknown objects within our solar system especially difficult.

According to recent reports, euclid intentionally avoids the region of the sky surrounding the plane of the solar system, where large numbers of asteroids and comets can be found. Dust concentrated in this region produces unwanted light that could interfere with the telescope's sensitive observations of the distant universe.

Industry observers note that the spacecraft also follows a 'step-and-stare' observing strategy, typically imaging each section of the sky only once. This means researchers cannot readily direct Euclid back toward a newly detected comet to gather more information about it.

Identifying objects within our solar system is nevertheless an key part of Euclid's scientific work. Researchers must account for everything appearing in its images so that unrelated features, including comet trails and unwanted light, can be removed without compromising the accuracy of its galaxy measurements.

"Very few comets are expected to be discovered by Euclid so it was a happy coincidence that the combination of the comet's orbit and Euclid's scanning over those days captured the object in multiple images," says Bruno Altieri, Euclid Archive Scientist, and part of the discovery team.

Preparing for a Future Comet Encounter.

Euclid's unexpected discovery also provides valuable experience for scientists working on ESA's future Comet Interceptor mission. Although the newly identified comet is not an appropriate destination for the spacecraft, the successful detection and rapid notification process demonstrates how the two missions could work together to identify potential targets.

Industry observers note that "While this particular comet is not a suitable candidate for Comet Interceptor, the process of discovery and alert gives us a real test case for how our two mission teams will coordinate in the future. And we are of course happy to have discovered a previously unknown comet for the Solar System community to follow-up on," adds Valeria Pettorino, Euclid Project Scientist.

Ancient Remnants of the Solar System.

Comets are ancient bodies composed of ice and dust that remain from the formation of our solar system approximately 4.6 billion years ago. Most originate in the distant Kuiper Belt and Oort Cloud, regions located beyond the orbits of the outer planets (interstellar comets come from other solar systems).

Industry observers note that as a comet approaches the Sun, increasing temperatures cause its ice to turn directly into gas. Escaping gas and dust form a glowing, fuzzy cloud known as a 'coma,' as well as an extended tail.

In a recent development, because comets native to our solar system have remained relatively unchanged since their formation, they preserve valuable evidence of the materials and environmental conditions that existed when the planets were taking shape. Studying these ancient objects may also help scientists understand the origins of Earth's water and the chemical building blocks of life.

Euclid's Hunt for Dark Matter and Dark Energy.

In a recent development, the primary goal of the Euclid mission is to uncover how dark matter and dark energy influence the visible universe. During its six-year survey, the space telescope will examine the shapes and movements of billions of galaxies at distances reaching up to 10 billion light-years.

The comet discovery was reported on behalf of the Solar System Objects Science Working Group of the Euclid Consortium by M. Pöntinen, A. A. Nucita, A. Franco, M. Granvik, B. Altieri, S. Kruk, B. Y. Irureta-Goyena and B. Carry.

Natalie Tran is turning short-form comedy into a filmmaking career

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2656 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Natalie Tran had already spent most of her life performing by the time one of her videos unexpectedly took off online.
  • She started acting at five, first through musical theater and later through commercials and indie films.
  • Industry observers note that then, at the end of 2023, one of her videos went viral.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Natalie Tran had already spent most of her life performing by the time one of her videos unexpectedly took off online.

She started acting at five, first through musical theater and later through commercials and indie films. Content creation came much later — initially as something she did for fun, not as an attempt to build an audience.

Industry observers note that then, at the end of 2023, one of her videos went viral. "I was gaining so many followers, I couldn't even believe it," Tran told Mashable at VidCon 2026.

Sources indicate that but going viral was only the beginning. Tran took the comedic persona and format that audiences responded to and kept building, eventually turning short-form sketches into another arm of a career that still revolves around her original love: acting. Now she's trying to bring those worlds even closer together.

Sources indicate that tran recently wrapped Passion Project, a roughly 17-minute short film she wrote, directed, produced, and acted in, with hopes of using it as a proof of concept for a future feature. And rather than seeing her years making social video as separate from filmmaking, she indicates the skills she developed online — from finding the hook to obsessing over an edit — made directing feel surprisingly familiar.

"It feels like one of my skits, just higher budget," she noted.

For Mashable's Creator Playbook, Tran talks about what happens after a viral moment, why short-form comedy taught her to be a better filmmaker, the changing relationship between creators and Hollywood, and why sometimes ambition just has to be louder than insecurity.

Mashable: You started acting when you were five. How did content creation eventually enter the picture?

Natalie Tran: I auditioned for a play called The King and I because I'd always been singing. That's actually where I started — as a singer. Surprisingly, I'm mainly an actor now, but I thought I was going to be a singer initially.

I got into musical theater and, from there, moved on to commercial work, indie films, all that jazz. That's what led me into content creation because I really like performing. I like making funny videos, things like that. I'd been making videos here and there, but never to get an audience, just kind of for fun.

Industry observers note that at the very tail end of 2023, I made a video that went viral. It blew up, and then I kind of took the bit and ran with it. Now I'm here. It's been interesting to see how acting and content creation can work together. Every day I'm kind of building that brand and making it work.

According to recent reports, anyone can have a viral video. What did you do after yours took off to turn that moment into something bigger?

Sources indicate that at first, I was just shocked. I was like, "There's no way this is happening." I was gaining so many followers; I couldn't even believe it. Then I started making videos. My favorite thing ever is when people comment that I'm funny. I love being called funny. It's my favorite compliment. That made me really happy to be recognized for that because I'm actually a pretty shy person. I like that I'm now recognized for my personality.

Sources indicate that I think I can show my personality not just through my videos, but also when I direct something, make movies, or do long-form work. It's also helped me become a more sociable person in general. Everything kind of works together to build my career.

Your comedy works really well in short-form. Do you think those skills translate to long-form filmmaking?

Definitely. I just wrapped a short film, and that'll be about 17 minutes. The goal is for that to be a proof of concept for feature films in the future.

According to recent reports, I think short-form has really helped me because, you know, how in school there's always a word count? They're like, "Get below the word count." You can get the idea faster. With short-form, it's: Get the audience hooked in the first three seconds. I think that still applies to long-form because you want to make it engaging.

Now that I have this short-form experience, I can kind of be like, "OK, this can be a bunch of different short ideas that I can stitch together." That's kind of how I think about it now.

How much intention goes into those first three seconds?

Industry observers note that when I make a video, I make sure my face is the first thing they see. I think about high energy right away. Maybe not the best joke — you want to keep the punchline for the end — but you want to have something really engaging.

Recent findings suggest that you think of an idea and then ask, "OK, what can make it even funnier? What's going to make someone stop scrolling and be like, 'Oh, I want to watch this whole video?'" Sometimes it sucks because it's like, "I don't want to have to make the first thing a clickbait reaction." So it's a matter of thinking about what's worth it.

According to recent reports, there's a balance. You don't want to draw your audience in and then have the rest of the video be something they didn't actually want to watch.

Why do you think comedy works so well in short-form?

Recent findings suggest that the biggest thing about comedy is timing, and that's really vital with shorts. It's like boom, boom, boom. I'm a very percussive comedian, I would say. I'm so picky with the edit.

According to recent reports, it depends because I also love comedy that's dry — no edit, literally nothing. But then I also love the comedy where it's cut, cut, cut, cut, cut. That's why it does so well in short-form. With these short attention spans, it works because it keeps you engaged the whole time.

According to recent reports, tell me about Passion Project. What made you finally decide to write and direct something yourself?

Recent findings suggest that I've been acting since I was young, and people would ask me a lot, "Do you ever want to write or direct something?" And I would think, "Yeah, yeah, yeah." Then I was in a feature film last year called Frogman Returns, and I was really drawn to the way it was shot. It was a lot of one-ers, and I saw the way the actor chemistry worked on camera.

It was generating ideas, so I came up with the idea of Passion Project on that set. It was very early stages, but I remember I still have the voice memo where I was like, "Oh my gosh, it could be this thing where it's a lot of one-ers and really good actors.".

Recent findings suggest that acting is the main thing. That's my love. I sat on it for half a year. Then over winter break, my friend was at a party, and she said, "Natalie, someone has the same idea as you." And I went, "Nope. That's not gonna happen. I'm making it.".

According to recent reports, that was the kick in the butt I needed to start writing it. It was about five months of pre-production and rewrites, and then we shot it in May. It was a dream come true. I'd been on camera a lot and worked as an actor my whole life, but this was my first time really being the producer, director, and writer behind everything. I found that I really love it.

How did being a content creator prepare you to direct a film?

In a recent development, I asked in my producing class one day, "Have you ever had a director who is also an actor in it?" Because everyone wants to say that it's very hard to direct and act in your own movie. I disagree.

Industry observers note that the reason is because I have all this content creation experience where I'm filming with a friend, I ask them to record me, I watch the playback, I go, "OK, redo it. Change the angle. I'm gonna change my acting." And that's exactly how it was on set. I kept telling everyone, "This feels like one of my skits, just higher budget.".

Content creation helped me so much because I already had that acting background, but filming my skits and finding out what I like in my own videos really helped me. Now I know how to communicate that to a team.

Industry observers note that there used to be this idea that creators used the internet as a stepping stone to Hollywood. Does that distinction still feel relevant to you?

Industry observers note that I think it's a lot easier now. I think it's the time where creators are bursting out of their bubble. Before, it was hard to get discovered. I'm lucky because I did have the traditional acting background, but now that I'm able to put my own stuff out there, it's an extra push.

Because of that, I'm able to put myself out there. I've gotten with a great agency and management, and all these things have been helping me build my career.

It has been revealed that it's a really interesting time. I feel like a lot of people didn't expect it to be this way. It's growing every day, and more people are talking about creators getting into Hollywood.

It has been revealed that social following is even becoming part of traditional casting now. How have you seen those worlds collide?

I'll get auditions now, and sometimes they'll ask for your socials. I just think that's interesting, how it's a factor now. It's hit-or-miss because you don't want to cast people solely for their following, of course.

Industry observers note that with Passion Project, I purposely sought out creators who are actors but also do content because that's where I come from. It was really fun to have that room of people who had the same understanding of this industry. People recognize the faces in the movie, but I'm not just hiring any Joe Schmo off the internet. I had a casting process as well. It's interesting to see how those worlds collide.

Sources indicate that acting and content creation used to feel like two separate sides of your career. Do they still?

It has been revealed that when I started social media, it was almost a battle. If you even look at my Instagram feed, I had my pictures and it was all acting, modeling, acting, modeling. Then you swipe over and it's me being like — what is this weird juxtaposition?

Before, it was kind of battling with each other. Now I'm learning to marry the two and really have them work together.

Authenticity gets talked about constantly in creator spaces. How do you stay authentic when so much of your content is satirical?

Recent findings suggest that I blew up kind of for satirical videos, and a lot of people got it. They were like, "Oh, I know you're not actually like that." And then some people thought I was like that, and I'm like, "Wait, but now I'm not being authentic." It's hard. I consider myself pretty multifaceted. I'll livestream, and I never really like to play characters in my livestream. I'll do accents all the time — I love to do an accent — but I'm not gonna fake stuff.

Sources indicate that that's where my authenticity comes from. I'm always gonna be real. Someone asks me a question, I'll answer real. I'm not gonna give you a fake answer. It can get difficult with content because you do want to play things up sometimes for the video. But luckily, since I come from the sketch comedy world, it's always going to be a bit. You can tell it's not real.

What do you think keeps people coming back to your content?

In a recent development, I think it's how weird I am. I talk in accents all the time. My manager literally went, "Who is this?" It's just fun. I like putting on silly voices and making weird faces and just being myself on camera. But it's also funny because when people meet me in real life, they're like, "Oh, you're way more chill." It comes out in bursts. I think that's what makes my videos fun.

What's your advice for someone who's scared to put themselves out there?

According to recent reports, just put yourself out there. If you are confident in what you do, just do it. Don't care about what other people think. And I'm saying that, and I do care about what other people think. I get scared to post things sometimes because I'm scared of people thinking it's stupid or commenting something mean.

But luckily, I think my drive is higher than my insecurity. I don't know what to call it. Put yourself out there, because if you're passionate about what you do — I've used the word passion over and over again, especially because of Passion Project — it's gonna pay off. If you love what you do, it's worth it to pursue it.

Do you still read the comments?

In a recent development, when I first blew up, I would read every single comment. Even on the video that I always talk about that blew me up — I think that one got over 20 million views — I think I literally read every comment. I was on my phone because it's a dopamine rush. It's honestly pretty shocking initially.

Industry observers note that now I've gotten to the point where once in a while I'll check my DMs or look at the comments. It depends on my mood. There are some videos where maybe I've read every comment. There are some videos where I don't think I even opened the comment section. I'm kind of sporadic.

Do those metrics mean less to you now than they used to?

Yes. I think I'm more prone to looking at the comments on videos that I'm really proud of because those are always really nice. But there are some videos — and I don't make these as much anymore — that were a little more rage bait. A lot of the comments were mean, and so I take one look, and I'm like, "Never mind. I'm done.".

In a recent development, there are days when I'll open my comment section, and it ruins my day. That'll happen. That's another piece of advice to creators. I'm one to say it because I do let it ruin my day sometimes, but try not to. That's all you can do.

So: have fun, put yourself out there, don't get consumed by the comments or views, and maybe do a funny little accent.

Do a funny little accent. Everyone will love it.

Crystal Bell is the Digital Culture Editor at Mashable, where she leads coverage of the creator economy, internet culture, and digital life. Her work focuses on the people, platforms, and communities shaping modern entertainment, from YouTube creators and livestreamers to fandoms, social media trends, and the evolving relationship between technology and culture. She also oversees the Mashable 101, the publication's annual list recognizing the internet's most influential creators.

It has been revealed that previously, she was the entertainment director at MTV News, where she helped expand the brand's coverage of fan culture, K-pop, and the internet's most passionate communities. Her work has appeared in Teen Vogue, Rolling Stone, PAPER, NYLON, ELLE, Glamour, NME, W, The FADER, and elsewhere on the internet.

Sources indicate that she's exceptionally fluent in fandom and will gladly make you a K-pop playlist and/or provide anime recommendations upon request. Crystal lives in New York City with her two black cats, Howl and Sophie.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen say they are continuing their attacks on Saudi Arabia, claiming to have damaged a key oil refinery as well as the petromonarchy's financial district in the capital Riyadh.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree on Wednesday mentioned that "accurate and direct" attacks targeting Ras Tanura — Saudi Arabia's largest oil refinery and a major export terminal for crude — had "caused fires to break out at the facility.".

Saree noted an attack on Saudi Arabia's financial district, located in the capital Riyadh, was "carried out in three phases, with strikes hitting their targets accurately.".

Saudi defense officials noted that air defenses in the kingdom had taken down four Houthi drones at Ras Tanura and that 11 people had been injured when a tower in the financial district was hit.

The building in question was also targeted on November 19, but no one was injured in that attack.

The Houthis and Saudis have been fighting for over a decade as part of a civil war that has become a regional conflict with increased significance as a result of the ongoing conflict in Iran and the Strait of Hormuz.

Tech Report: International first class is over for U.S. airlines. Enter the mega business-class cabin

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1122 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the era of U.S.
  • airlines have been ditching international first-class cabins for a fresh top tier: larger and souped-up business classes, featuring suites with sliding doors, the design du jour.
  • In a recent development, many travelers might not notice the difference.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the era of U.S. airlines' long-haul, international first class ended this week when American Airlines' last flight with its eight-suite section landed. In its place will be a massive business-class cabin with room for 70 passengers.

It has been revealed that U.S. airlines have been ditching international first-class cabins for a fresh top tier: larger and souped-up business classes, featuring suites with sliding doors, the design du jour. Delta Air Lines and United Airlines have already taken this step. American was the last of the U.S. airlines to still have first class on long-haul international routes.

In a recent development, many travelers might not notice the difference. That's because of airlines' investments into business class: fresh suites, bigger screens, better technology like device-charging pads, and improved bedding.

It's part of airlines' substantial bet on mass luxury. Consumers have been willing to shell out more to fly comfortably, which is helping to boost airline revenue. That's all the more important as costs of everything from fuel to airport landing fees have been rising, soaking up more of the industry's profits.

The retirement of first class ends a more-than-six-decade stretch of the jet age that in the early days included service like seat-side carving of chateaubriand and meals served on fine bone china.

A few decades ago, business class was much smaller, with two-by-two seats in some configurations, and recliners, not the lie-flat seats that dominate those cabins now.

"When you've got individual pods in biz class, and you've got a comfortable enough seat and bedding and decent wine, for a lot of people this is good enough," stated Henry Harteveldt, founder of travel consulting firm Atmosphere Research Group and a former airline executive.

The over-the-top dining of the early days of international first class was a form of entertainment, long before laptops, personal seat-back screens and in-flight Wi-Fi, or even the promise of sleep on lie-flat beds, but customers still eat lots on board, Harteveldt said.

"People say they want to sleep but then they stay up and they eat every morsel," he said. "They're hypocrites.".

There was still a hefty price gap between first and business.

A flight between Los Angeles and London on American's Boeing 777-300ER this week went for $12,994 in business class for a one-way ticket and $15,669 for a first-class seat.

American's last flight with international first class departed Friday morning local time in Sydney, bound for Los Angeles.

In a recent development, its latest cabin on its Boeing 777-300ERs will feature 70 business-class suites, the most of any U.S. airline. Pre-overhaul, the cabins had been operating with eight first-class suites and 52 pods in business, though the remodeling is ongoing. American is also flying a subfleet of 787-9 Dreamliners that have 51 business-class suites. (United is putting 64 new suites on that aircraft.).

Part of the allure is that some companies allow employees to book business-class tickets, but not first class.

American Airlines told CNBC it's growing its business-class cabins across the fleet. It's evaluating increasing the number of suites on its smaller long-haul jets, the Boeing 787-8 Dreamliners, from 20 currently to somewhere in the 30s.

"You don't have enough seats to make the seat cost competitive," Nat Pieper, American's chief commercial officer, mentioned in an interview this month. "So what you need to do to make that airplane work is it's got to be a yield play. You need more business-class seats.".

Differences between first and business classes on American lately came down to details.

On American's first-class long-haul section, passengers got olives with warm nuts to accompany their beverage early in the flight, while there were no olives for business class.

Recent findings suggest that first class got a soup; business did not. First class got a warm dessert served a la mode in addition to the cold dessert or fruit and cheese plate both cabins were offered.

And there was no memory foam lumbar pillow for business class like there was in first, American mentioned. But otherwise, the experiences were fairly similar for passengers. They still got better food options and service than economy passengers, along with their bigger seats, early boarding and lounge access.

"It's not like the bed can go any flatter than 180 degrees," Harteveldt stated. "The bedding can be thicker, and the food nicer.".

Delta and United have already replaced international, long-haul first class with dozens of their Delta One and Polaris business lie-flat suites, respectively, each of which is getting upgrades now.

American will continue offering a separate lie-flat first class on its Airbus A321T subfleet it uses for domestic cross-country flying until early 2027. But then that goes away, too.

Meanwhile, airlines over the past decade have added a premium economy section, which sits between business class and economy. It features recliner seats similar to those in domestic first class, often with foot rests, meals served on actual plates, larger seat-back screens than economy and earlier boarding.

Airlines are now cutting up business class into different segments, something they've done for more than a decade with the coach cabin's basic economy, standard and extra legroom seats.

United and Delta this year each confirmed their most expensive cabins will be sold with basic options, which are more restrictive and don't include things like the ability to pick your seat ahead of time or get access to a special airport lounge.

Industry observers note that there are also a few seats in some of the business-class cabins that are roomier, like American's Flagship Suite Preferred and United's Polaris Studio. Even the guest seating in the United suite varies with "standard and companion ottomans," the latter including a seatbelt so you can ask "another Polaris passenger to visit you between takeoff and landing for a drink, chat or game," the airline says.

"I don't think we found the limit on segmentation," United CFO Mike Leskinen told CNBC on Thursday. "We have a few things on the drawing board. We're not done.".

Sources indicate that although U.S. carriers are moving away from the designation, first class is far from dead.

Singapore Airlines, Germany's Lufthansa, British Airways and Air France have unveiled updated first-class cabins and other service improvements like food.

British Airways last month said it will build a record 106-suite business class on its Airbus A380 aircraft, the world's largest passenger airplane, but it's also upgrading its first class on board.

Meanwhile, smaller airlines like JetBlue Airways, Frontier Airlines and Allegiant Air are introducing domestic or short-haul first-class seats.

"We're going to be able to do that at a really low price comparatively to what you're used to out there in the marketplace," Frontier Chief Commercial Officer Bobby Schroeter stated last month.

#104815. Hundreds of millions at risk from Chinese shopping app malware

📅 02 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1946 w)

General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 CNN ↗ Open Full Page

Hundreds of millions at risk from Chinese shopping app malware

📅 02 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1946 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It is one of China’s most popular shopping apps, selling clothing, groceries and just about everything else under the sun to more than 750 million owners a month.
  • But according to cybersecurity researchers, it can also bypass consumers’ cell phone security to monitor activities on other apps, check notifications, read private messages and change settings.
  • While many apps collect vast troves of user data, sometimes without explicit consent, experts say e-commerce giant Pinduoduo has taken violations of privacy and data security to the next level.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is one of China’s most popular shopping apps, selling clothing, groceries and just about everything else under the sun to more than 750 million owners a month.

But according to cybersecurity researchers, it can also bypass consumers’ cell phone security to monitor activities on other apps, check notifications, read private messages and change settings.

And once installed, it’s tough to remove.

While many apps collect vast troves of user data, sometimes without explicit consent, experts say e-commerce giant Pinduoduo has taken violations of privacy and data security to the next level.

In a detailed investigation, CNN spoke to half a dozen cybersecurity teams from Asia, Europe and the United States — as well as multiple former and current Pinduoduo employees — after receiving a tipoff.

Recent findings suggest that multiple experts identified the presence of malware on the Pinduoduo app that exploited vulnerabilities in Android operating systems. Manufacturer insiders stated the exploits were utilized to spy on users and competitors, allegedly to boost sales.

“We haven’t seen a mainstream app like this trying to escalate their privileges to gain access to things that they’re not supposed to gain access to,” said Mikko Hyppönen, chief research officer at WithSecure, a Finnish cybersecurity firm.

“This is highly unusual, and it is pretty damning for Pinduoduo.”.

Malware, short for malicious software, refers to any software developed to steal data or interfere with computer systems and mobile devices.

Evidence of sophisticated malware in the Pinduoduo app comes amid intense scrutiny of Chinese-developed apps like TikTok over concerns about data security.

Some American lawmakers are pushing for a national ban on the popular short-video app, whose CEO Shou Chew was grilled by Congress for five hours last week about its relations with the Chinese government.

In a recent development, the revelations are also likely to draw more attention to Pinduoduo’s international sister app, Temu, which is topping US download charts and fast expanding in other Western markets. Both are owned by Nasdaq-listed PDD, a multinational company with roots in China.

While Temu has not been implicated, Pinduoduo’s alleged actions risk casting a shadow over its sister app’s global expansion.

It has been revealed that there is no evidence that Pinduoduo has handed data to the Chinese government. But as Beijing enjoys significant leverage over businesses under its jurisdiction, there are concerns from US lawmakers that any tech giant operating in China could be forced to cooperate with a broad range of security activities.

The findings follow Google’s suspension of Pinduoduo from its Play Store in March, citing malware identified in versions of the app.

An ensuing report from Bloomberg remarked a Russian cybersecurity firm had also identified potential malware in the app.

Pinduoduo has previously rejected “the speculation and accusation that Pinduoduo app is malicious.”.

CNN has contacted PDD multiple times over email and phone for comment, but has not received a response.

Pinduoduo, which boasts a user base that accounts for three quarters of China’s online population and a market value three times that of eBay (EBAY), wasn’t always an online shopping behemoth.

Founded in 2015 in Shanghai by Colin Huang, a former Google employee, the startup was fighting to establish itself in a market long dominated by e-commerce stalwarts Alibaba (BABA) and JD.com (JD).

It succeeded by offering steep discounts on friends-and-family group buying orders and focusing on lower-income rural areas.

Recent findings suggest that pinduoduo posted triple digit growth in monthly users until the end of 2018, the year it listed in New York. By the middle of 2020, though, the increase in monthly users had slowed to around 50% and would continue to decline, according to its earnings reports.

It was in 2020, according to a current Pinduoduo employee, that the organization set up a team of about 100 engineers and product managers to dig for vulnerabilities in Android phones, develop ways to exploit them — and turn that into profit.

According to the source, who requested anonymity for fear of reprisals, the manufacturer only targeted consumers in rural areas and smaller towns initially, while avoiding users in megacities such as Beijing and Shanghai.

“The goal was to reduce the risk of being exposed,” they said.

By collecting expansive data on user activities, the company was able to create a comprehensive portrait of consumers’ habits, interests and preferences, according to the source.

This allowed it to improve its machine learning model to offer more personalized push notifications and ads, attracting consumers to open the app and place orders, they said.

The team was disbanded in early March, the source added, after questions about their activities came to light.

PDD didn’t reply to CNN’s repeated requests for comment on the team.

Approached by CNN, researchers from Tel Aviv-based cyber firm Check Point Research, Delaware-based app security startup Oversecured and Hyppönen’s WithSecure conducted independent analysis of the 6.49.0 version of the app, released on Chinese app stores in late February.

Sources indicate that google Play is not available in China, and Android people in the country download their apps from local stores. In March, when Google suspended Pinduoduo, it remarked it had found malware in off-Play versions of the app.

The researchers found code designed to achieve “privilege escalation”: a type of cyberattack that exploits a vulnerable operating system to gain a higher level of access to data than it’s supposed to have, according to experts.

“Our team has reverse engineered that code and we can confirm that it tries to escalate rights, tries to gain access to things normal apps wouldn’t be able to do on Android phones,” remarked Hyppönen.

Recent findings suggest that the app was able to continue running in the background and prevent itself from being uninstalled, which allowed it to boost its monthly active user rates, Hyppönen said. It also had the ability to spy on competitors by tracking activity on other shopping apps and getting information from them, he added.

Check Point Research additionally identified ways in which the app was able to evade scrutiny.

The app deployed a method that allowed it to push updates without an app store review process meant to detect malicious applications, the researchers said.

They also identified in some plug-ins the intent to obscure potentially malicious components by hiding them under legitimate file names, such as Google’s.

“Such a technique is widely used by malware developers that inject malicious code into applications that have legitimate functionality,” they said.

In China, about three quarters of smartphone customers are on the Android system. Apple (AAPL)’s iPhone has 25% market share, according to Daniel Ives of Wedbush Securities.

Sergey Toshin, the founder of Oversecured, stated Pinduoduo’s malware specifically targeted different Android-based operating systems, including those used by Samsung, Huawei, Xiaomi and Oppo.

CNN has reached out to these companies for comment.

Toshin described Pinduoduo as “the most dangerous malware” ever found among mainstream apps.

“I’ve never seen anything like this before. It’s like, super expansive,” he said.

Most phone manufacturers globally customize the core Android software, the Android Open Source Project (AOSP), to add unique features and applications to their own devices.

In a recent development, toshin found Pinduoduo to have exploited about 50 Android system vulnerabilities. Most of the exploits were tailor made for customized parts known as the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) code, which tends to be audited less often than AOSP and is therefore more prone to vulnerabilities, he stated.

Sources indicate that pinduoduo also exploited a number of AOSP vulnerabilities, including one which was flagged by Toshin to Google in February 2022. Google fixed the bug this March, he said.

Sources indicate that according to Toshin, the exploits allowed Pinduoduo access to owners’ locations, contacts, calendars, notifications and photo albums without their consent. They were also able to change system settings and access users’ social network accounts and chats, he noted.

According to recent reports, of the six teams CNN spoke to for this story, three did not conduct full examinations. But their primary reviews showed that Pinduoduo asked for a large number of permissions beyond the normal functions of a shopping app.

They included “potentially invasive permissions” such as “set wallpaper” and “download without notification,” said René Mayrhofer, head of the Institute of Networks and Security at the Johannes Kepler University Linz in Austria.

It has been revealed that suspicions about malware in Pinduoduo’s app were first raised in late February in a report by a Chinese cybersecurity firm called Dark Navy. Even though the analysis didn’t directly name the shopping giant, the report spread rapidly among other researchers, who did name the organization. Some of the analysts followed up with their own reports confirming the original findings.

Soon after, on March 5, Pinduoduo issued a fresh enhancement of its app, version 6.50.0, which removed the exploits, according to two experts who CNN spoke to.

Two days after the update, Pinduoduo disbanded the team of engineers and product managers who had developed the exploits, according to the Pinduoduo source.

Sources indicate that the next day, team members found themselves locked out of Pinduoduo’s bespoke workplace communication app, Knock, and lost access to files on the company’s internal network. Engineers also found their access to substantial data, data sheets and the log system revoked, the source said.

According to recent reports, most of the team were transferred to work at Temu. They were assigned to different departments at the subsidiary, with some working on marketing or developing push notifications, according to the source.

A core group of about 20 cybersecurity engineers who specialize in finding and exploiting vulnerabilities remain at Pinduoduo, they said.

Toshin of Oversecured, who looked into the update, stated although the exploits were removed, the underlying code was still there and could be reactivated to carry out attacks.

Pinduoduo has been able to grow its user base against a backdrop of the Chinese government’s regulatory clampdown on Big Tech that began in late 2020.

That year, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology introduced a sweeping crackdown on apps that illegally collect and use personal data.

In 2021, Beijing passed its first comprehensive data privacy legislation.

In a recent development, the Personal Information Protection Law stipulates that no party should illegally collect, process or transmit personal information. They’re also banned from exploiting internet-related security vulnerabilities or engaging in actions that endanger cybersecurity.

Pinduoduo’s apparent malware would be a violation of those laws, tech policy experts say, and should have been detected by the regulator.

In a recent development, “This would be embarrassing for the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, because this is their job,” mentioned Kendra Schaefer, a tech policy expert at Trivium China, a consultancy. “They’re supposed to check Pinduoduo, and the fact that they didn’t find (anything) is embarrassing for the regulator.”.

Industry observers note that the ministry has regularly published lists to name and shame apps found to have undermined user privacy or other rights. It also publishes a separate list of apps that are removed from app stores for failing to comply with regulations.

Pinduoduo did not appear on any of the lists.

CNN has reached out to the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and the Cyberspace Administration of China for comment.

On Chinese social media, some cybersecurity experts questioned why regulators haven’t taken any action.

“Probably none of our regulators can understand coding and programming, nor do they understand technology. You can’t even understand the malicious code when it’s shoved right in front of your face,” a cybersecurity expert with 1.8 million followers wrote last week in a viral post on Weibo, a Twitter-like platform.

The post was censored the next day.

CNN’s Kristie Lu Stout and Sean Lyngaas contributed reporting.
